absolute uncertainty: The uncertainty in a measurement expressed in the same units as the measured value.
accuracy and precision: Accuracy is closeness to the true value, while precision is how closely repeated measurements agree.
best-fit line and extreme gradients: A method that uses the steepest and shallowest lines within error bars to find the uncertainty in a graph's gradient.
derived units: Units built from combinations of base units, such as the newton or joule.
dimensional homogeneity: The principle that both sides of a valid physical equation must have the same units or dimensions.
drift angle: The angle between an object's intended direction and its actual path when moving through a flowing medium.
error bars: Lines on a graph point showing the range of uncertainty in a measured value.
fractional / percentage uncertainty: The absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value, often expressed as a percentage.
free fall: Motion under gravity alone, with air resistance neglected, giving an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2.
gradient uncertainty: The uncertainty in a best-fit line's gradient, found from the spread of the extreme gradients.
half the smallest division: The estimated absolute uncertainty of an analog instrument, equal to half its smallest scale division.
intercept: The point where a linear graph crosses the y-axis, which can reveal systematic error.
linearization: Rearranging a non-linear relationship into a straight-line form for analysis.
projectile motion: Two-dimensional motion in which horizontal and vertical components act independently, linked only by time.
random error: An error that varies unpredictably between measurements and can be reduced by averaging.
relative velocity: The velocity of an object as observed from a particular reference frame.
resultant vector: The single vector obtained by adding two or more vectors.
scalar: A quantity described fully by magnitude alone, with no direction.
si base units: The seven fundamental units of the International System from which all other units are derived.
si prefixes: Abbreviations representing powers of ten attached to units, such as kilo, milli, and micro.
significant figures / significant digits: The meaningful digits of a measurement that convey its precision.
standard form / scientific notation: A way of writing numbers as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten.
suvat variables: The five quantities (displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time) describing uniformly accelerated motion.
systematic error: An error that shifts all measurements in the same direction, removable only by improved design or calibration.
uncertainty / error: The range within which a measured value may differ from the true value.
uniform acceleration: Motion in which acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction.
vector: A quantity having both magnitude and direction.
vector resolution: Splitting a vector into two perpendicular components using sine and cosine.
vector triangle: A geometric method representing the sum of vectors as the sides of a triangle, often for equilibrium.
acceleration: The rate of change of velocity with time; a vector quantity.
apparent weight: The normal reaction force a scale reads, which changes when a body accelerates vertically.
area under v-t graph: The area beneath a velocity-time graph, equal to the displacement.
average velocity & instantaneous velocit: Average velocity is total displacement over time; instantaneous velocity is the slope at a single instant.
conservation of mechanical energy: The principle that kinetic plus potential energy stays constant when no non-conservative forces act.
direction of net force and acceleration: The fact that net force and acceleration always point in the same direction.
displacement: The vector giving the straight-line distance and direction from start to finish.
elastic collision: A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
free-body diagram, fbd: A diagram showing a single object and all the forces acting on it as arrows.
friction: The contact force opposing relative motion between surfaces, either static or kinetic.
impulse, j: The product of force and the time it acts, equal to the change in momentum.
maximum height: The highest point of a projectile, where its vertical velocity is zero.
momentum, p: The product of an object's mass and velocity; a vector quantity.
newton's first law — law of inertia: The law that an object with zero net force stays at rest or moves at constant velocity.
newton's second law: The law that the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration.
newton's third law — action-reaction: The law that forces between two bodies are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
normal force, n: The contact force a surface exerts perpendicular to itself on an object.
perfectly inelastic collision: A collision in which objects stick together, conserving momentum but losing the most kinetic energy.
power, p: The rate of doing work, measured in watts.
system approach: Analyzing connected bodies as a single system to find their common acceleration before finding internal forces.
tension, t: The pulling force transmitted through a string, rope, or cable.
time of flight: The total time a projectile takes to return to its launch height.
work-energy theorem: The theorem that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
work, w: The product of force and displacement in the force's direction, a scalar measured in joules.
absolute zero: The lowest possible temperature, 0 K, at which molecular random motion ceases.
assumptions of an ideal gas: The simplifying assumptions, including point-mass molecules, no intermolecular forces, and perfectly elastic collisions.
boyle's law: At constant temperature, the pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional.
charles's law: At constant pressure, the volume of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature.
combined gas law & ideal gas equation: The relation PV/T constant and the ideal gas equation PV = nRT.
conservation of energy in mixing: In an insulated container, heat lost by a hot body equals heat gained by a cold body.
deviations from ideal behaviour: Departures of real gases from ideal behavior at high pressure and low temperature.
gay-lussac's law: At constant volume, the pressure of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature.
heat transferred: The heat Q = mc(delta T) needed to change a substance's temperature.
heat, q: Energy transferred between bodies because of a temperature difference; a process quantity.
heating/cooling curve: A graph of temperature versus heat, with sloped regions for temperature change and plateaus for phase change.
internal energy, u: The total random kinetic and intermolecular potential energy of a body's particles.
molecular interpretation of phase change: The view that heat during a phase change breaks intermolecular bonds rather than raising temperature.
molecular origin of pressure: The idea that gas pressure arises from molecules colliding with and transferring momentum to container walls.
specific heat capacity, c: The heat needed to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one kelvin.
specific latent heat, l: The heat needed to change the state of one kilogram of a substance without a temperature change.
temperature: A measure of the average random kinetic energy of a substance's particles.
temperature and mean kinetic energy: The relation that a gas molecule's average kinetic energy is proportional to its absolute temperature.
thermal equilibrium: The state in which two bodies in contact have the same temperature and no net heat flows.
zeroth law of thermodynamics: The law that if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other.
amplitude, a: The maximum displacement of an oscillation from its equilibrium position.
antinode: A point of maximum amplitude in a standing wave, where constructive interference always occurs.
blueshift: A shift of light to shorter wavelengths when a source moves toward the observer.
diffraction: The spreading of a wave as it passes around an obstacle or through a slit.
doppler effect: The change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other.
doppler formula sign convention: The rules for choosing signs in the Doppler formula based on motion toward or away.
frequency, f: The number of oscillations per unit time, measured in hertz, equal to the reciprocal of the period.
fundamental: The lowest frequency standing-wave pattern on a string or in a pipe.
intensity, i: The power passing through unit area, proportional to amplitude squared.
longitudinal wave: A wave in which particle vibration is parallel to the direction of travel, such as sound.
path difference: The difference in distance traveled by two waves, determining constructive or destructive interference.
polarization: Restricting the vibration of a transverse wave to a single direction.
ray: A line perpendicular to a wavefront showing the direction of energy travel.
resonance: A large increase in amplitude when a driving frequency matches a system's natural frequency.
simple harmonic motion, shm: Oscillation in which the restoring force is proportional to and opposite the displacement.
snell's law: The relation n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2) describing refraction between media.
standing wave: A stationary wave pattern formed by two opposite waves, with fixed nodes and antinodes.
total internal reflection: Complete reflection of light at a boundary when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
transverse wave: A wave in which particle vibration is perpendicular to the direction of travel, such as light.
wave speed, v: The speed at which a wave transfers energy, equal to frequency times wavelength.
x-t graph vs. x-position graph: A displacement-time graph reveals the period, while a displacement-position graph reveals the wavelength.
charge carriers: The mobile charged particles, such as electrons or ions, that constitute an electric current.
circular motion in magnetic field: The circular path of a charged particle moving perpendicular to a magnetic field, with radius r = mv/(qB).
conservation of charge: The principle that the total electric charge in an isolated system remains constant.
coulomb's law: The law giving the electrostatic force between two point charges as proportional to their product over the square of their separation.
electric field lines: Curves visualizing an electric field, pointing from positive to negative charge and never crossing.
electric field, e: The force per unit positive charge at a point in space.
electric potential: The electric potential energy per unit charge at a point in a field.
electrical energy: The energy delivered or consumed by an electrical component, given by P = VI times time.
force between parallel wires: The attractive or repulsive force per unit length between two current-carrying parallel wires.
force on a current-carrying conductor: The force F = BIL sin(theta) on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.
internal resistance, r: The resistance within a source itself, causing the terminal voltage to fall below the emf when current flows.
kirchhoff's laws: The current law (charge conservation at junctions) and the voltage law (energy conservation around loops).
magnetic field lines: Closed curves visualizing a magnetic field, running from a magnet's north pole to its south pole.
resistivity, ρ: A material's intrinsic opposition to current, relating resistance to a conductor's length and cross-section.
series and parallel connections: Two ways of connecting components, with current shared in series and voltage shared in parallel.
superposition principle: The principle that the net force on a charge is the vector sum of the individual Coulomb forces.
uniform electric field: A field of constant magnitude and direction, such as that between two parallel charged plates, where E = V/d.
centripetal acceleration, a: The acceleration directed toward the center of a circular path, equal to v^2/r.
centripetal force, f_c: The net inward force required for circular motion, equal to mv^2/r.
conical pendulum: A pendulum whose bob moves in a horizontal circle while the string traces a cone.
escape speed: The minimum speed needed to escape a planet's gravity, equal to the square root of 2GM/R.
geostationary satellite: A satellite orbiting above the equator with a 24-hour period so it appears fixed over one point.
gm/r: The orbital speed of a circular orbit, equal to the square root of GM/r, independent of the satellite's mass.
gravitational field strength, g: The gravitational force per unit mass at a point, equal to GM/r^2.
gravitational potential energy, ep: The energy -GMm/r of a mass in a gravitational field, taking infinity as the zero reference.
newton's law of universal gravitation: The law that every two masses attract with a force proportional to their product over the square of their separation.
orbital energy analysis: The study of a satellite's kinetic, potential, and total energy, the total being negative for a bound orbit.
period, t: The time for one full revolution, related to angular velocity by T = 2 pi over omega.
antiparticles: Particles with the same mass but opposite charge to their corresponding particles, such as the positron.
comparison of radiation types: A comparison of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation by penetrating power and ionizing ability.
conservation laws summary: The requirement that particle reactions conserve charge, baryon number, and lepton number.
emission/absorption spectrum: An emission spectrum shows bright lines from emitted photons; an absorption spectrum shows dark lines from absorbed ones.
feynman diagrams: Diagrams that qualitatively represent particle interactions and the exchange particles involved.
fission, fusion & be curve: Energy release from splitting heavy nuclei or fusing light ones, explained by the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve.
four fundamental forces & exchange parti: The strong, weak, electromagnetic, and gravitational forces and their respective exchange particles.
hadrons: Particles made of quarks, divided into three-quark baryons and quark-antiquark mesons.
hydrogen spectral series: Groups of hydrogen spectral lines named by the lower energy level reached, such as the Lyman and Balmer series.
mass defect & binding energy: The mass lost when nucleons bind, equal via E = mc^2 to the nucleus's binding energy.
nuclear notation & decay equations: The notation for nuclei and the balanced equations describing alpha, beta, and gamma decay.
photon: A quantum of light emitted or absorbed when an electron changes energy levels, with energy E = hf.
quantisation: The principle that an atom's electrons can only have specific discrete energy levels.
albedo feedback & climate feedback: Climate feedback loops, such as melting ice lowering albedo and amplifying warming.
conduction: Heat transfer through a material by particle collisions, without bulk movement of matter.
convection: Heat transfer in a fluid caused by density differences driving the fluid to move.
energy balance perturbation: A disturbance to Earth's energy balance, such as radiative forcing, that shifts the equilibrium temperature.
greenhouse gases: Atmospheric gases that absorb and re-emit long-wave infrared radiation, warming the surface.
planck curve: The spectral distribution of radiation emitted by a black body at a given temperature.
primary & secondary energy sources: Primary sources are taken directly from nature; secondary sources like electricity are converted from them.
renewable & non-renewable energy sources: Renewable sources replenish faster than used, while non-renewable sources are effectively finite.
sankey diagram & efficiency: A diagram showing energy flows by arrow width, used to illustrate efficiency and losses.
solar constant, s₀: The solar radiation per unit area received perpendicular to the Sun just outside Earth's atmosphere, about 1360 W/m^2.
specific energy & energy density: Specific energy is energy stored per unit mass; energy density is energy stored per unit volume.
wien's displacement law & emissivity: Wien's law relates a black body's peak wavelength to its temperature; emissivity scales a real body's emission.
